title: The Covering and the Element: a Norman Grammarian Reads the World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Conches-en-Ouche, the name that outlasts the record
stops.date_confidence: traditional; English scholarship gives c. 1085-1090, French scholarship c. 1080, and no source gives a month or a day. The year here is the midpoint of the English range and carries no authority of its own.
stops.campa: A boy is born in the Ouche country of Normandy, in or near the small town whose name he will carry through every manuscript that survives him. No baptismal entry and no charter records the birth. The accounts come centuries after the fact and they disagree: one tradition puts it around 1080, another between 1085 and 1090, and both allow that the village may not have been Conches at all. What the record keeps is the toponym. The next thing said about him has him already grown and already sitting in a schoolroom at Chartres.
suggested_refs: The town of Conches-en-Ouche in the diocese of Evreux, from which he takes the only name any source gives him
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (c. 1085-1090, 'generally taken to have been Conches though possibly nearby Tilleul')
French Wikipedia, 'Guillaume de Conches' (ne autour de 1080)

stops.name: Saint-Martin-du-Tilleul, the other village
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Tilleul is offered by one source as a possible birthplace alongside Conches, with no date attached and no document behind either.
stops.campa: Some thirty miles west of Conches, near Bernay, a second village holds a second claim on him. English scholarship allows that he may have come from Tilleul rather than from Conches, and it is at Tilleul, not at Conches, that a twelfth-century funeral slab will be turned up seven centuries later. Between them the two villages hold both ends of his life, a birth at one or the other and a grave at one or the other, and no document decides either. He is named for a town he may never have lived in.
suggested_refs: Saint-Martin-du-Tilleul, Eure, formerly Tilleul-Follenfant, the alternative birthplace and the site of the tomb slab
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' ('possibly nearby Tilleul')
French Wikipedia, 'Saint-Martin-du-Tilleul' (commune article, former name Tilleul-Follenfant)

stops.name: Evreux, the diocese and the missing schoolroom
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source names him at Evreux at any date. The year is a placeholder for boyhood schooling that must have happened somewhere and is nowhere recorded.
stops.campa: Conches lies in the diocese of Evreux, and whatever schooling a Norman boy got before the cathedral schools of the Ile-de-France, he got inside this bishopric. Nothing names him here. No cartulary of the chapter lists him, and the reachable sources say nothing at all about what teaching the cathedral of Evreux offered in these decades. So what can be marked here is a diocese and not a schoolroom, the administrative fact that the country of his birth answered to this church. Where he learned his letters is not known.
suggested_refs: The cathedral of Notre-Dame d'Evreux, seat of the diocese containing Conches
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (birthplace given as a village near Evreux)
French Wikipedia, 'Cathedrale Notre-Dame d'Evreux' (contains nothing on an eleventh- or twelfth-century cathedral school; recorded as a gap)

stops.name: Chartres, the school of Bernard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact of the studentship, reconstructed for the year. Bernard of Chartres is documented at the school only by 1115 and holds the chancellorship until 1124; no source dates William's arrival within that window.
stops.campa: He comes south to the cathedral school of Chartres and sits under Bernard, the master whose whole teaching runs through grammar as the road into everything else: read the poets closely enough and the physics falls out of the syntax. Bernard is documented at the school by 1115 and chancellor until 1124, which fixes a window; nothing fixes the year inside it. What he takes from Bernard is the method he will use for the next forty years, the slow gloss, one text opened word by word across a whole term of teaching.
suggested_refs: The cathedral close of Chartres under Bernard, chancellor of the school until 1124
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (studied under Bernard of Chartres)
English Wikipedia, 'Bernard of Chartres' (at the school by 1115, chancellor to 1124)
John of Salisbury, Metalogicon I.5

stops.name: Blois, following the master
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the sources place Bernard's teaching at Chartres and Blois both and place William under Bernard, but no source states that William was at Blois in any particular year.
stops.campa: Bernard taught at Blois as well as at Chartres, and the accounts that put William under him put him in both places, a pupil following a man rather than enrolling in an institution. There is no register to enroll in. The schools of this generation are masters, not buildings; where the master goes the school goes, and the students go with him along the Loire. Blois survives as a name inside a sentence about Bernard, and William's presence in the town is drawn out of that sentence and out of nothing firmer.
suggested_refs: Blois, second site of Bernard of Chartres's teaching
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' ('studied under Bernard of Chartres in Chartres and Blois')

stops.name: Chartres, the pupil takes the chair
stops.date_confidence: attested as a period, c. 1115-1120, not as a year. The change from student to master is nowhere dated or documented.
stops.campa: Between 1115 and 1120 he stops being a student and becomes a master, teaching grammar and the arts in the same close where he had construed Priscian under Bernard. The transition is unceremonious and unrecorded: no charter appoints him and no bishop licenses him in any surviving document. What survives is that by the 1120s students are coming to him. For the next twenty years his name is attached to two cities, Paris and Chartres, and no source consulted says which of the years belong to which of them.
suggested_refs: The masters' schools of the Chartres cathedral close in the 1110s and 1120s
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (teaching career begins c. 1115-1120, based primarily in Paris and Chartres)

stops.name: Chartres, the glosses on Priscian
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the two editions of the Priscian commentary are securely his, but neither their dates nor the place of composition is attested. Chartres is where he is otherwise known to have been.
stops.campa: He writes commentaries on Priscian's Institutiones grammaticae, and then writes them again: two separate editions of the same book, the mark of a man teaching the same text year after year and changing his mind about it. The gloss treats grammar as a discipline capable of carrying arguments about the nature of things and not merely rules for the ordering of words. What a noun is turns out to be a question about what a thing is. Both editions are securely his. Neither carries a date, and neither says where it was written.
suggested_refs: The Glosae super Priscianum, surviving in two authorial editions
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' ('2 editions of his own commentary on Priscian's Institutes of Grammar')
Editions and commentary of Edouard Jeauneau and Lodi Nauta

segments.name: Paris, and the Book of the World

stops.name: Paris, the cloister schools of the island
stops.date_confidence: attested that his career was based primarily in Paris and Chartres; unattested for any year, address, or duration in Paris.
stops.campa: His teaching career is described as based primarily in Paris and Chartres, and in Paris the schools cluster in the cathedral cloister on the island, a loose federation of masters under the chancellor's licence that will take another century to harden into a university. He lectures somewhere in that crowd. No source names his classroom, his lodging, his students there, or the years. The city holds him only as the second half of a phrase, Paris and Chartres. How much of a working life that phrase covers, and when, is a question the record does not answer.
suggested_refs: The cathedral cloister schools of Notre-Dame de Paris before the incorporation of the university
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' ('primarily based in Paris and Chartres')

stops.name: Mont Sainte-Genevieve, the hill outside the licence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction only. No source places William on the Mount; the stop is inferred from where independent masters of his generation taught.
stops.campa: On the left bank hill beyond the city wall, masters of his generation teach clear of the chancellor's licence and outside the chapter's reach. Abelard taught there. It is where a man goes who wants students and does not want a canon's permission to have them, and it fits what is known of William's independence. But nothing places him on the Mount. The record puts him in Paris and then goes quiet about the address, and this stop is inference from the institutional habit of the era. No source consulted names him here.
suggested_refs: The schools of Mont Sainte-Genevieve, where masters taught outside the cathedral chapter's control
sources: General pattern of early twelfth-century Paris masters, Abelard and his contemporaries; no source consulted names William of Conches here

stops.name: Chartres, the Philosophia mundi
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 1125-1130 as a period; the year is chosen inside that range and the place of composition is not attested at all.
stops.campa: He writes the Philosophia mundi, four books running from the elements to the human soul, taking in physics, astronomy, geography, meteorology and medicine as one continuous account of how the world is put together. Behind it stand Plato's Timaeus in Calcidius's Latin, Macrobius, and the medical texts Constantine the African had turned out of Arabic into Latin a generation earlier. He will later expand it to six books. Sixty-eight manuscripts of the first version survive, and sixteen of the second.
stops.quote: Elementum ergo, ut ait Constantinus in Pantegni, est simpla et minima pars alicuius corporis, simpla ad qualitatem, minima ad quantitatem.
stops.quote_source: William of Conches, Philosophia mundi I.22
suggested_refs: The Philosophia mundi in its four-book and six-book recensions; Paul Edward Dutton's manuscript census
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
Migne, Patrologia Latina 172 (printed among the works of Honorius Augustodunensis)
Marco Albertazzi, critical edition of the Philosophia (2007)

stops.name: Chartres, the elements no eye has seen
stops.date_confidence: attested as text, undated as an event. The chapter belongs to the Philosophia mundi, composed c. 1125-1130.
stops.campa: Earth, water, air and fire, the four bodies a man can point at, are not the elements. They are elementata, things built out of elements. The elements themselves are the simplest and least parts of any body, simple in quality and minimal in quantity, and they are never seen at all; reason arrives at them by dividing, and only reason. He takes the definition from Constantine's Pantegni and carries it further than Constantine does, into a physics of invisible particles taught aloud in a cathedral close. The chapter is the twenty-first of the first book, written somewhere in the second half of the 1120s.
stops.quote: Haec elementa nunquam videntur, sed ratione divisionis intelliguntur.
stops.quote_source: William of Conches, Philosophia mundi I.21 (Patrologia Latina 172, col. 48ff.)
suggested_refs: Constantine the African's Pantegni, the Latin gateway through which Arabic medicine reached the Chartres masters
sources: Migne, Patrologia Latina 172
Maurice de Wulf, History of Mediaeval Philosophy
Friedrich Ueberweg, Grundriss der Geschichte der Philosophie

stops.name: Chartres, the answer to the ignorant
stops.date_confidence: attested as text at Philosophia mundi I.23; undated as an event, and the chapter's own composition falls somewhere in c. 1125-1130.
stops.campa: Partway through the first book he stops explaining and turns on his critics. They do not know the forces of nature themselves, he writes, and wanting company in their ignorance they would rather nobody looked into anything: let us believe like peasants and not ask the reason. His own position is that the reason of all things may and must be sought, Genesis included, and that seeking it takes nothing whatever away from God. The sentence circulates widely in English, in a rendering behind which no named translator and no critical edition stands.
stops.quote: Sed quoniam ipsi nesciunt vires naturae, ut ignorantiae suae omnes socios habeant, nolunt eos aliquid inquirere, sed ut rusticos nos credere nec rationem quaerere.
stops.quote_source: William of Conches, Philosophia mundi I.23 (Patrologia Latina 172, col. 56)
suggested_refs: Marie-Dominique Chenu, Nature, Man, and Society in the Twelfth Century, which supplies the locus for the passage
sources: Marie-Dominique Chenu, Nature, Man, and Society in the Twelfth Century (trans. Taylor and Little)
Reginald Lane Poole, Illustrations of the History of Medieval Thought and Learning
Tina Stiefel, The Intellectual Revolution in Twelfth-Century Europe
French Wikipedia, 'Guillaume de Conches' (on seeking the reason of all things, Genesis included)

stops.name: Chartres, glossing Plato's Timaeus
stops.date_confidence: attested as a work, dated only to the 1130s by modern scholarship; the place of composition is inferred from his known base.
stops.campa: He works line by line through the Timaeus in Calcidius's Latin, the only Plato the Latin West possesses, and produces the Glosae super Platonem. The dialogue Plato composed at Athens and named for a Locrian becomes, in a French schoolroom sixteen centuries on, a textbook of physics with one theological problem lodged at its centre. Plato's craftsman god fits a Christian creator well enough. The soul he sets turning inside the world does not fit the Holy Spirit, and William will not leave the question alone.
suggested_refs: The Glosae super Platonem, ed. Edouard Jeauneau; Calcidius's partial Latin Timaeus, the West's whole access to Plato
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
Edouard Jeauneau, edition of the Glosae super Platonem
Elford, 'William of Conches', in Dronke, A History of Twelfth-Century Western Philosophy

stops.name: Chartres, the integumentum
stops.date_confidence: attested as a method throughout his commentaries; not datable to a year. The year here sits alongside the Timaeus glosses of the 1130s and carries no authority of its own.
stops.campa: His instrument for the pagan texts is the integumentum, the covering. A fable scandalous on its face, gods coupling and warring and lying, is a wrapping laid over a truth that could not be said plainly at the time; strip the covering and the philosophy underneath stands there orthodox. Read by an unfriendly reader, the method is also a licence to make any text say whatever its commentator wants it to say. It lets him teach Plato, Macrobius and Juvenal inside a cathedral school without apologising for them, and he uses it on all three.
suggested_refs: The doctrine of integumentum as practised by the Chartrain commentators
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
Elford, 'William of Conches', in Dronke, A History of Twelfth-Century Western Philosophy

stops.name: Chartres, glossing Boethius, Macrobius, Juvenal
stops.date_confidence: attested as works, spread across the 1120s to 1150s; individual dates and places of composition are not recoverable.
stops.campa: Alongside Priscian and Plato he glosses Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio, and Juvenal's Satires. Together the commentaries make a course rather than a shelf: grammar first, then the shape of the cosmos, then the question of how a man is to live inside it. He teaches out of these books for a working lifetime, and students copy them and lend them onward. Individual dates and places of composition are not recoverable for any one of them.
suggested_refs: The Glosae super Boetium and the glosses on Macrobius and Juvenal
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (list of works)
Editions and commentary of Lodi Nauta and Paul Edward Dutton

stops.name: Chartres, John of Salisbury in the lecture room
stops.date_confidence: attested; the sources give 1137-1138 for John of Salisbury's study under William at Chartres.
stops.campa: An Englishman in his twenties comes to Chartres and sits in William's lectures for the better part of two years. The Metalogicon, written decades afterwards, records that William was pushed off Bernard's slow method by a crowd of the unlearned, the party John of Salisbury names Cornificians, who wanted the arts taught quickly and cheaply. The censure falls on them and not on the master, of whom John writes: gramaticus post Bernardum Carnotensem opulentissimus, the most richly gifted grammarian after Bernard of Chartres.
stops.quote: Willelmus de Conchis, gramaticus post Bernardum Carnotensem opulentissimus.
suggested_refs: John of Salisbury, Metalogicon I.5, the single richest contemporary witness to William's teaching
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (taught John of Salisbury at Chartres, 1137-1138)
Edouard Jeauneau, Lectio philosophorum: recherches sur l'Ecole de Chartres (citing Metalogicon 1,5)
John Howle Newell, The Dignity of Man in William of Conches and the School of Chartres

stops.name: Chartres, the world-soul and the third person
stops.date_confidence: attested that the identification is in his work and that it drew the attack of 1141; the year here brackets the controversy rather than dating an event.
stops.campa: The identification he has made in the Glosae and in the Philosophia, the Platonic world-soul with the Holy Spirit, is the sentence his enemies have been waiting for. Read one way it is an ornament of the integumentum, a pagan covering laid over a Christian truth. Read another way it makes the third person of the Trinity into a function of the cosmos, which is modalism, which is heresy. In the schools of 1141 it is the second reading that travels. William of Saint-Thierry, reading in the Ardennes, takes it that way.
suggested_refs: The world-soul passages of the Glosae super Platonem and the Philosophia mundi, the substance of the 1141 charge
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
Elford in Dronke, A History of Twelfth-Century Western Philosophy
R. W. Southern, Medieval Humanism

stops.name: Signy-l'Abbaye, the letter written
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1141; no month or day is given in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: In his Cistercian retreat in the Ardennes, William of Saint-Thierry, once an abbot and now a monk by choice, reads the Philosophia and writes a letter cataloguing its errors. Later tradition titles it De erroribus Guillelmi de Conchis. Its charge is the world-soul and the Trinity; its request is that the recipient move against this William as he has already moved against Abelard. The letter's own Latin could not be reached for this file. What is known of its contents comes through secondary paraphrase and nothing else.
stops.quote_source: Title, in later tradition, of William of Saint-Thierry's letter of 1141
suggested_refs: William of Saint-Thierry, De erroribus Guillelmi de Conchis, written from Signy in 1141
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Saint-Thierry' (letter addressed to Bernard in 1141)
English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'

stops.name: Clairvaux, the letter received
stops.date_confidence: attested for the addressing of the letter to Bernard of Clairvaux in 1141; entirely unattested for anything Bernard did about it.
stops.campa: The letter goes to Bernard of Clairvaux, who in this same year is prosecuting Peter Abelard and needs no persuading that dialectic turned on the Trinity is a danger. Whether Bernard answers it, acts on it, or does anything at all about William of Conches is not recorded anywhere reachable. No condemnation follows: no council summons him, no sentence is pronounced, no retraction is demanded in any surviving act. The accusation is documented. What came of it is not, and the gap there is a real one rather than a tactful silence.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Bernard of Clairvaux for 1141, in which no reply concerning William of Conches has been identified
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Saint-Thierry'
English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
bernard_clairvaux.journey.json (Bernard's campaign against Abelard, same year)

stops.name: Sens, the council that condemns Abelard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the council and for Abelard's condemnation; William of Conches's presence is not attested and is not claimed here.
stops.campa: At Sens, Abelard is condemned and his writings with him. William is not there, and no source puts him there. What Sens supplies is the temperature of the year: in this country, at this moment, a master who reads the physical world as intelligible on its own terms and says so in Latin is a man with a problem. The two cases are separate cases, sharing no charge, no accuser and no court. Bernard of Clairvaux prosecuted the one and received the letter about the other, in the same year.
suggested_refs: The Council of Sens, 1141, and the condemnation of Peter Abelard's writings
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
General historical record of the Council of Sens; no source consulted places William there

stops.name: Chartres, the schoolroom closes
stops.date_confidence: attested that he withdrew from public teaching after 1141; the year 1142 is a placeholder, and no source dates the withdrawal.
stops.campa: He stops teaching in public. There is no prosecution to withdraw from, no verdict, no recantation demanded in any surviving act; there is an accusation, a hostile climate, and a career that ends. Whatever passed between him and the authorities passed without leaving a document behind it. What is visible afterwards is a man past fifty with no schoolroom, revising his own books toward safer formulations and looking for a patron who is not a bishop.
suggested_refs: The absence of any conciliar or episcopal act against William of Conches, in contrast to the record for Abelard
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (withdrew from public teaching after 1141)
R. W. Southern, Medieval Humanism

stops.name: Angers, the count's protection
stops.date_confidence: attested that he entered the service of Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou, c. 1143-1144; the location is reconstruction, since no source names where.
stops.campa: Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou, takes him into the household. The arrangement is attested and the place is not; Angers is the count's principal seat rather than anywhere a source actually sets William down. The exchange is plain enough from both sides. A count acquires the most accomplished grammarian in France to teach his sons their letters. A philosopher under suspicion of modalism acquires a lay lord's roof, which no letter sent to Clairvaux can reach through. The castle a visitor climbs to at Angers now was raised between 1230 and 1242.
suggested_refs: The comital seat of Anjou at Angers under Geoffrey Plantagenet; the surviving chateau there postdates him by a century
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (sought the protection of Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou; no location given)
French Wikipedia, 'Chateau d'Angers' (present castle built 1230-1242, therefore not Geoffrey's court)

stops.name: Le Mans, the household on circuit
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Henry's birth at Le Mans in 1133 is attested, William's presence in the city is not attested at any date.
stops.campa: Henry Plantagenet, the elder pupil, was born at Le Mans in 1133 and is ten or eleven years old when William takes him in hand. An Angevin comital household is not a house but a circuit, moving between Angers and Le Mans and, from 1144, Rouen, with the tutor and the schoolbooks moving along with it. What the boy is taught, in what language, out of which books, no source records; the tutorship is a fact with no curriculum attached. No source places William at Le Mans either. The itinerary here is the one a household tutor necessarily kept, drawn from the job and not from a document.
suggested_refs: Le Mans, birthplace of Henry Plantagenet in 1133 and a principal seat of the Angevin circuit
sources: General historical record of Henry II's birth at Le Mans, 1133
English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (tutor to Henry Plantagenet, c. 1143-1144; no place given)

stops.name: Rouen, the duke's sons
stops.date_confidence: attested for the tutoring of Henry's brothers from 1146 to 1149 and for Geoffrey's ducal accession in 1144; the location Rouen is reconstruction, unmentioned in the sources on William.
stops.campa: Geoffrey enters Rouen in January 1144 and takes the ducal title of Normandy that summer, and the household's weight shifts north into the duchy. From 1146 to 1149 William tutors the younger brothers, Geoffrey and William. The eldest is already away at his own business and will be king of England within ten years. Rouen stands sixty miles from Conches, so the old grammarian is teaching the sons of the man who now rules the country he was born in. Whether he ever went back to look at it, no source says.
suggested_refs: The ducal seat at Rouen under Geoffrey Plantagenet from 1144
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (tutored Henry's brothers 1146-1149)
Standard record of Geoffrey Plantagenet's entry into Rouen, 14 January 1144, and ducal title that summer

stops.name: Rouen, the Dragmaticon philosophiae
stops.date_confidence: attested only to a range, sometime between 1144 and 1149; the single year is a placeholder inside that range and the place of composition is not attested at all.
stops.campa: He rewrites the Philosophia as a dialogue between a philosopher and a duke and calls it the Dragmaticon. It runs to roughly twice the length of the original and drops only a few pages of it, taking in more Greek and Arabic material than the first book could hold. The dedication goes to Geoffrey Plantagenet under his Angevin title, Count of Anjou, and not under the newer Norman one. It is written somewhere between 1144 and 1149. The five years cannot be narrowed, and the room cannot be named at all.
suggested_refs: Italo Ronca's critical edition of the Dragmaticon philosophiae (1997), with the English Dialogue on Natural Philosophy
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (Dragmaticon, between 1144 and 1149, dedicated to Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou)
Italo Ronca, ed., Dragmaticon philosophiae, CCCM (1997)

stops.name: Rouen, the sentence taken back
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Dragmaticon softens the earlier Trinitarian formulations; the year is a placeholder within 1144-1149 and no source dates the revision.
stops.campa: In the new book the identification that drew the letter is gone, softened out or simply not made. He has not stopped holding that the reason of things may be sought; the Dragmaticon inquires into nature as freely as the Philosophia ever did, distinguishing what God does by his will alone from what he does through nature as the instrument of the divine working. He has stopped saying the one sentence about the world-soul that could be read as heresy. Prudence, a change of mind, or the terms of an agreement nobody wrote down: the record does not say.
stops.quote: Dieu gouverne le monde par l'intermédiaire de l'ordre naturel
stops.quote_source: Guillaume de Conches, as quoted in French Wikipedia, 'Guillaume de Conches'; underlying Latin and translator not identified in the source
suggested_refs: The Dragmaticon's revised treatment of the world-soul, set beside the Philosophia's
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches'
French Wikipedia, 'Guillaume de Conches' (God acting by his will alone, and through nature as instrument of the divine operation)

stops.name: Conches-en-Ouche, the French date
stops.date_confidence: traditional; French scholarship gives death around 1150 or a little after, at Conches-en-Ouche, explicitly flagging the dates as approximate. The stops in this segment run in date order, earliest tradition first.
stops.campa: French scholarship puts the death around 1150 or a little after, at Conches-en-Ouche itself, in the town whose name he had carried since he was a student. The source that gives the dates calls them approximate in the same breath. Nothing supports the siting except the tradition that keeps it: no obit, no necrology entry, no twelfth-century notice of any kind. It is the earliest of the three answers the record offers, and the only one that ends him inside the toponym he had been travelling under for seventy years.
suggested_refs: The French tradition of death at Conches-en-Ouche c. 1150, absent from English accounts
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Guillaume de Conches' ('mort vers 1150 ou peu apres (dates approximatives) a Conches-en-Ouche en Normandie')

stops.name: Paris, the English date
stops.date_confidence: traditional; English scholarship gives 1154 or shortly afterward and offers Paris only as one of two possibilities, without choosing.
stops.campa: English scholarship gives a different decade: dead in 1154 or shortly after, and the place named first is Paris. If that is right he ends in the city of the schools he was pushed out of thirteen years before. Nothing supports it except its own repetition. There is no obit, no necrology entry, no letter of condolence, no notice from any of the students who must still have been alive to write one. His books were copied in the hundreds. His death is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The absence of any twelfth-century notice of William of Conches's death, in Paris or anywhere else
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' ('died in 1154 or shortly afterward, probably at Paris or the environs of Evreux')

stops.name: Evreux, the alternative in the same sentence
stops.date_confidence: traditional; offered by the same source as Paris, as the alternative half of an unresolved 'or'.
stops.campa: The English sentence that offers Paris offers the country around Evreux as the alternative, and declines to choose. If this one is right he went home: back to the Ouche, to the diocese he was born in, some seventy years and sixty miles from where he started, in the last years of the ducal household that had sheltered him. The two places sit side by side, joined by the word or and given equal weight. So three accounts stand unreconciled, Conches around 1150, Paris and the Evreux countryside in 1154 or after. No source consulted adjudicates.
suggested_refs: The diocese of Evreux as the alternative death-place in the English tradition
sources: English Wikipedia, 'William of Conches' (death location given as Paris or the environs of Evreux)

stops.name: Saint-Martin-du-Tilleul, the church that is gone
stops.date_confidence: traditional for the burial, which no document records; the year is a placeholder set just after the latest death date offered.
stops.campa: At Tilleul stood the church of Saint-Germain, parish church of the hamlet of Tilleul-Follenfant, marked on the cadastral survey of 1850 and standing no longer. Nothing is there to see now. He is said to have been laid there, in a Norman village of no consequence whatever, rather than at Chartres or in Paris where he had spent his working life. A twelfth-century funeral slab carrying an effigy came out of the ground on that site in 1857, and the notice published on it that year concluded that the grave beneath was his.
stops.quote: il s'agirait effectivement de la sepulture ou repose Guillaume de Conches
stops.quote_source: Antoine Charma, notice of 1857 on the slab found at Saint-Martin-du-Tilleul

stops.name: Conches-en-Ouche, the slab in Sainte-Foy
stops.date_confidence: undated; no source records when, or whether, the slab was moved. The year given is that of the first modern notice, not of any translation.
stops.campa: Inside the church of Sainte-Foy at Conches-en-Ouche lies a twelfth-century tombstone of Guillaume de Conches. English accounts state flatly that the funeral slab with his effigy was moved here from Tilleul. French accounts record the stone in the church and narrate no move at all, and no source consulted claims his body was ever carried anywhere. The slab is there and can be looked at. That the man cut into it is him rests on Charma's conditional verdict of 1857 and on nothing else.

stops.name: Conches-en-Ouche, six centuries under other men's names
stops.date_confidence: attested; the correct attribution is established in Oudin's Commentarius, published 1722, five years after Oudin's own death in September 1717.
stops.campa: The Philosophia goes on being copied and stops being his. Manuscripts hand it to Bede, to William of Hirsau, to Honorius of Autun; the printers follow the manuscripts, and it ends up in the Patrologia among the works of Honorius, where a reader can still find it. The name comes back in 1722, in the Commentarius de scriptoribus ecclesiae antiquis of Remi-Casimir Oudin, published at Leipzig five years after Oudin himself was dead. Charles Jourdain in 1838 and Jean-Barthelemy Haureau in 1858 finish the restitution.

stops.name: Conches-en-Ouche, the books counted
stops.date_confidence: attested; the editions are dated individually and Ronca's Dragmaticon appears in 1997.
stops.campa: Paul Edward Dutton's census counts sixty-eight surviving manuscripts of the original Philosophia and sixteen of the six-book revision. The critical editions run from Carmelo Ottaviano in 1935 and Joseph-Marie Parent in 1938 through Edouard Jeauneau in 1957 and 1965, Gregor Maurach in 1974 and 1980. The last of them is Italo Ronca's Dragmaticon of 1997, a Corpus Christianorum edition printing the Latin and an English rendering on facing pages, under the author's own name, eight centuries after the manuscripts stopped carrying it.
